solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Stop early input behind fighting (3,2,3,3)

indicatorNotes.fighting: letters that are fighting are thrashing about, so they land in a new order

annotation.surface: Someone putting their oar in from the back of a brawl, only to be cut short.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Input behind' reads like a phrase in its own right, which hides that its eleven letters are exactly the answer's.
annotation.definitionFit: To nip something in the bud is to stop it at an early stage, before it can flower.

entries.clue: Write up hack for relative (6)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, going up reads the letters bottom to top

blocks.note: to hew = to hack, as with an axe

annotation.surface: A writer being told to knock out some copy for a family member.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hack' pulls towards journalism next to 'write', but here it is chopping.
annotation.definitionFit: A nephew is a relative: your sibling's son.

entries.clue: Maybe we spurn Napoleon or revolutionary (8,7)

indicatorNotes.revolutionary: a revolution overturns the order of things, here the letters

annotation.surface: A choice between turning your back on Napoleon or on some revolutionary.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' tells you 'we' is one example of the answer; the history-lesson surface makes 'we' look like the start of a sentence rather than the thing defined.
annotation.definitionFit: 'We' is a personal pronoun, standing for the speaker and others.

entries.clue: Cover of NME list includes German song and English one (6,4)

indicatorNotes.Cover of: the cover of a word is its outside, its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.includes: one piece takes the other inside it

blocks.note: a ship lists or leans to one side
a Lied is a German art song, placed inside LEAN after its L

annotation.surface: The front page of the NME printing a chart with a German song and an English one on it.
annotation.walkthrough: The NME is a British music paper, so 'list' looks like a chart; it is the verb for a ship tilting. 'One' in the definition means a song, picked up from 'German song'.
annotation.definitionFit: Nellie Dean is an English music-hall song, the old pub singalong 'Sweet Nellie Dean'.

entries.clue: Be repelled by odd characters among hearties (4)

indicatorNotes.odd characters among: take the letters in the odd positions, 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th

annotation.surface: Someone recoiling from the strange types in a crowd of jolly sailors.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Odd characters' looks like eccentric people among the hearties, but it means the odd-numbered letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: loathing something means recoiling from it, the verb sense of the definition.

entries.clue: Composer, older composer, uncovered problem in organ (9)

indicatorNotes.uncovered: strip the cover off a word: remove its first and last letters

blocks.note: J S Bach, far older than the answer
EARACHE is a problem in an organ, the ear; without its outer letters it leaves ARACH

annotation.surface: A list of composers ending with a fault inside a church organ.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Organ' sits next to Bach and says pipe organ; it is the ear. Burt Bacharach is the American songwriter of 'Walk On By'.
annotation.definitionFit: Burt Bacharach was a composer of popular songs.

entries.clue: Mark cleaned bottles in dump (7)

indicatorNotes.bottles in: to bottle something in is to hold it inside

blocks.note: 'I did the dishes' = I cleaned them
a scar is a mark left on the skin

annotation.surface: Mark tidied up and bottled things up before a trip to the tip.
annotation.walkthrough: Read it as '[a] mark [that] cleaned bottles in': DID holds SCAR. 'Mark' looks like a man's name, and DID for 'cleaned' is the everyday 'did the washing-up'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean getting rid of something unwanted, like a card thrown away from a hand.

entries.clue: Registered offender wrote for cast? (11)

blocks.note: writing lines for actors is scripting; the ? flags the loose definition-by-example

annotation.surface: A registered sex offender who has become a playwright.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Registered offender' reads as one phrase, but 'Registered' is the definition standing alone, in its sense of enrolled for military service.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone conscripted has been registered, enrolled compulsorily, for military service.

entries.clue: One takes off top first or second batsman after about noon (3-6)

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for noon
the first two batsmen in a cricket innings are the openers

annotation.surface: A cricket scene: an opening batsman going in shortly after midday.
annotation.walkthrough: The cricket makes 'takes off top' sound like a batsman hitting the bowler for six; the top is the lid of a tin.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the tool's whole job is removing lids, so 'one takes off top' describes it by what it does.

entries.clue: Bill suppressing love shows restraint? (5)

indicatorNotes.suppressing: one word holds another down inside it

blocks.note: a bill is a beak, a nose

annotation.surface: A parliamentary bill that curbs affection turns out to be a restraining measure.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bill' says legislation, next to 'restraint'; it is a bird's beak. The ? admits a noose is a grim sort of restraint.
annotation.definitionFit: A noose is a loop that restrains, tightening as it is pulled.

entries.clue: Something eccentric surrounding male attached to extremely glamorous tight dress (9)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: CAM goes around everything that follows
indicatorNotes.extremely: take the extremes, first and last letters

blocks.note: a cam is an eccentric wheel in an engine

annotation.surface: An odd character wrapped around a man in a clingy, glamorous frock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Something eccentric' suggests an oddball; an eccentric in engineering is an off-centre wheel, a CAM.
annotation.definitionFit: A cheongsam is a close-fitting Chinese dress with a high collar.

entries.clue: Helpful piece for the orchestra? (12)

blocks.note: the adjective: playing a useful part in bringing something about
the noun: a piece of music played without voices

annotation.surface: A useful bit of music written for the orchestra.
annotation.walkthrough: The ? marks the second sense as playful: an instrumental suits any band, not just an orchestra.
annotation.definitionFit: Being instrumental in something means being helpful to it; an instrumental is a piece for instruments.

entries.clue: Proud king traitor put up, one of five siblings (7)

indicatorNotes.put up: in a down clue, putting a word up writes it bottom to top

blocks.note: to rat on someone is to betray them
a quin is one of quintuplets

annotation.surface: A haughty monarch who has one of his quintuplet siblings sent up for treason.
annotation.walkthrough: Tarquin the Proud (Tarquinius Superbus) was the last king of Rome, so 'Proud' is part of his title, not an adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: Tarquin the Proud was the seventh and last legendary king of Rome.

entries.clue: Garden tool with ridges, its wrapper the wrong way round (6)

indicators: its wrapper the wrong way round

indicatorNotes.its wrapper the wrong way round: the wrapper is the outer pair of letters; swap them end for end

blocks.clueFragment: its wrapper the wrong way round
blocks.note: RIBBED with its outer R and D swapped

annotation.surface: A ridged garden tool that came in its packaging back to front.
annotation.walkthrough: Only the outside letters change places; the middle IBBE stays put.
annotation.definitionFit: A dibber is a pointed garden tool for making holes to plant seedlings.

entries.clue: Immobilised soldier left before large town overthrown (9)

indicatorNotes.overthrown: turned over, so the word reads backwards
indicatorNotes.before: one piece comes ahead of the next

blocks.note: a city is a large town

annotation.surface: A wounded soldier stuck in place while a city falls.
annotation.walkthrough: Paralytic is also British slang for blind drunk, which suits 'immobilised' too.
annotation.definitionFit: Paralytic means paralysed, unable to move.

entries.clue: Faint opportunity for action publicity man ultimately plugs (7)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: take the ultimate, last, letter of each word
indicatorNotes.plugs: the letters fill a hole in the other word

blocks.note: scope = room or opportunity to act

annotation.surface: A PR man grabbing a slim chance to act.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Faint' looks like an adjective for 'opportunity'; it is the noun, a fainting fit.
annotation.definitionFit: Syncope is the medical term for a faint, a brief loss of consciousness.

entries.clue: Plant hire periodically covered by advance payment (5)

indicatorNotes.periodically: at regular intervals, so every other letter
indicatorNotes.covered by: the other word goes over and around it

blocks.note: a sub is an advance on wages

annotation.surface: Renting machinery now and then, paid for up front.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Plant hire' is a real phrase for renting heavy machinery, so 'Plant' looks industrial; it is a bush.
annotation.definitionFit: A shrub is a woody plant smaller than a tree.

entries.clue: European Union starts to entice Norway, or so it seems (6)

indicatorNotes.starts to: take the start, first letter, of each following word

blocks.clueFragment: entice Norway, or so it seems
blocks.note: first letters of Entice Norway Or So It Seems

annotation.surface: The EU making overtures to Norway, which has always stayed outside it, or so it appears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'European Union' looks like the EU itself; it is a union within Europe, Cyprus with Greece.
annotation.definitionFit: Enosis was the movement for the union of Cyprus with Greece, a European union.

entries.clue: Yes, Silicon Valley giant circumvents American gall (3,5)

indicatorNotes.circumvents: to circumvent is literally to go around

blocks.note: A = American; it goes inside OK

annotation.surface: A tech giant nodding along while dodging American cheek.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gall' reads as nerve or cheek; here it is a growth on a tree.
annotation.definitionFit: An oak apple is a round gall on an oak, caused by a wasp larva.

entries.clue: Unexpected U-turn on train (7)

indicatorNotes.Unexpected: the letters come out in an unexpected order

annotation.surface: A railway train that suddenly reverses direction.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a railway noun; it is the verb, to bring up or educate.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of rearing: bringing up a child means shaping and educating it.

entries.clue: Uneducated Italian guy barely on top of tirade (8)

indicatorNotes.barely: stripped bare: the word loses its outer letters
indicatorNotes.on top of: in a down clue, the first piece sits above the second

blocks.note: SIGNOR, an Italian gentleman, without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: An ill-educated Italian who barely gets a word in over someone else's rant.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barely' looks like 'hardly'; it means bare the word, taking off its outside.
annotation.definitionFit: Ignorant means lacking knowledge or education.

entries.clue: Coward’s work terribly slammed in vacuous ding-dong with Ogden Nash (3,4,3,10)

indicatorNotes.vacuous: empty of its middle, leaving only the outer letters

annotation.surface: A Noël Coward piece savaged by critics in an empty-headed row with the poet Ogden Nash.
annotation.walkthrough: Coward and Nash were both writers of comic verse, so the literary feud is plausible. 'Ding-dong' is British slang for a row.
annotation.definitionFit: Mad Dogs and Englishmen is a comic song written by Noël Coward.

entries.clue: Displaced adult, ex criminal (7)

indicatorNotes.criminal: the letters are treated criminally, bent out of shape

annotation.surface: A grown-up former convict who has been uprooted.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ex criminal' reads as 'ex-criminal', a former offender; 'ex' is fodder and 'criminal' the indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: Luxated is a medical word for dislocated, displaced from its joint.

entries.clue: Blair’s language borders on naïve and feeble when hiding information for the better (8)

indicatorNotes.borders on: the borders of a word are its first and last letters
indicatorNotes.hiding: one word hides the other inside it

blocks.note: SP, the starting price, is what a bettor needs to know

annotation.surface: Tony Blair's political jargon, naïve and feeble, concealing facts to make things look better.
annotation.walkthrough: Blair is Eric Blair, George Orwell's real name, not Tony Blair. 'The better' is one who bets, and SP is the starting price of a horse.
annotation.definitionFit: Newspeak is the controlled language of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four.

entries.clue: Stupid person fled over high range (7)

blocks.note: a sop is a weak, silly person
O = over, as on a cricket scoresheet

annotation.surface: A fool running away across a mountain range.
annotation.walkthrough: 'High range' sounds like mountains after 'fled over'; it is a singing voice.
annotation.definitionFit: Soprano is the highest range of the singing voice.

entries.clue: Embarrassed female on ecstasy — that’s contemptible (8)

annotation.surface: Scorn for a woman left red-faced after taking a pill.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' only places SHE before E, reading downwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: looking meek and awkward like a sheep after a blunder is exactly how an embarrassed person looks.

entries.clue: Axeman’s curse has a hold on doctor in the Province (7)

indicatorNotes.has a hold on: one word holds the other inside it
indicatorNotes.in: the plain preposition: the doctor is placed inside the Province's two letters

annotation.surface: A murderer's curse gripping a doctor in Northern Ireland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Axeman' is slang for a guitarist, not a killer. 'The Province' is the usual British name for Northern Ireland.
annotation.definitionFit: Jimi Hendrix was the great rock guitarist, the ultimate axeman.

entries.clue: Having more of these, you’ll want more works on the radio (5)

annotation.definition: Having more of these, you’ll want more

indicatorNotes.on the radio: heard, not seen: go by the sound

blocks.note: kneads = works dough with the hands

annotation.surface: A sermon on how the more you get, the more you crave.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a riddle: needs are wants, so more needs means more wanting. 'Works' is kneading bread.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic definition: requirements are by nature wants, so piling up more of them leaves you wanting more.

entries.clue: Old army division of men receiving small amount of spirits (7)

indicatorNotes.receiving: one word takes the other in

blocks.note: a nip is a small measure of spirits

annotation.surface: A troop of soldiers being handed their tot of rum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Division of men' reads together, but the definition stops at 'division'.
annotation.definitionFit: A maniple was a subdivision of a Roman legion.

entries.clue: Literary hero in tricky situation beneath bird of prey (9,6)

indicatorNotes.beneath: in a down clue, the first piece sits under the second

blocks.note: in a pickle = in a fix

annotation.surface: A hero in a fix with a hawk circling overhead.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads in the reverse of the answer: PICKLE is beneath PEREGRINE, so the bird comes first.
annotation.definitionFit: Peregrine Pickle is the hero of Tobias Smollett's 1751 novel of that name.

entries.clue: Little island’s hallucinogen-yielding cactus out of bounds (4)

indicatorNotes.out of bounds: the bounds of a word are its ends; take them off

blocks.note: peyote is the cactus mescaline comes from
PEYOTE without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A tiny island where a drug-producing cactus is off limits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Out of bounds' sounds like forbidden; it means outside letters gone.
annotation.definitionFit: An eyot, or ait, is a small island in a river.

entries.clue: Goes fishing in outskirts of Flanders, unable to get a bite? (8)

indicatorNotes.in: one word goes inside the other
indicatorNotes.outskirts of: the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of Flanders
to angle is to fish with a rod

annotation.surface: An angler on the fringes of Flanders who cannot get a bite all day.
annotation.walkthrough: The fishing surface makes 'bite' a fish taking the bait; the definition means no teeth to bite with.
annotation.definitionFit: Fangless means without fangs, so unable to bite.

entries.clue: Eg set up cycling chart and get out of here (7)

indicatorNotes.set up: in a down clue, set up means written bottom to top
indicatorNotes.cycling: letters move round from the front to the back of the word

blocks.note: cycled so that CH goes round to the back: RTCHA

annotation.surface: A chart being wheeled round and someone being told to clear off.
annotation.walkthrough: Gertcha is London Cockney slang: 'get out of here!', a dismissive exclamation.
annotation.definitionFit: Gertcha is a Cockney rendering of 'get out of it', meaning clear off.

entries.clue: Mostly unreliable old military cover (5)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: most of the word: drop its last letter

annotation.surface: An army's defences that have mostly proved shaky.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Military cover' looks like air cover or protection; it is a hat.
annotation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall peaked military cap with a plume.

entries.clue: Reference book sign she unfortunately breaks (9)

indicatorNotes.breaks: the letters break into the other word

blocks.note: Taurus is a sign of the zodiac
SHE rearranged, placed after the T

annotation.surface: A woman unluckily snapping the spine of a book of signs.
annotation.walkthrough: Taurus is broken after its first letter, the T, to take HES.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Roget's book of synonyms is a standard volume to look words up in.

entries.clue: Topped Daliesque rubbish to settle score? (8)

indicatorNotes.Topped: with its top, the first letter, cut off
indicatorNotes.rubbish: the letters are made a mess of

annotation.surface: Surreal junk art, beheaded to get even with someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Settle score' sounds like revenge; in football, to equalise is to level the score.
annotation.definitionFit: To equalise is to score the goal that makes the scores level.

entries.clue: Copy electronic reminder to stop uproar (12)

indicatorNotes.to stop: the letters stop up, plug, the other word

blocks.note: a ruction is a noisy row
a prod is a nudge, a reminder

annotation.surface: An email nudge sent to calm an outcry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Stop' looks like calming an uproar; it means plugging the gap in a word. A ruction is British informal for a noisy quarrel.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a replica of a painting or piece of furniture, made to look like the original.

entries.clue: University official checks judge’s case for presentation aid? (9)

indicatorNotes.checks: to check something is to hold it back, so the official holds the letters inside
indicatorNotes.case: the case of a word is its outside, first and last letters

blocks.note: a proctor keeps discipline at a university

annotation.surface: A university disciplinary officer examining a legal case.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' and 'checks' make a courtroom or an investigation; they are containers here.
annotation.definitionFit: A projector throws slides onto a screen, an aid to presentations.

entries.clue: One way to make strong beer be distinctive (5,3)

annotation.definition2: One way to make strong beer

blocks.clueFragment: One way to make strong beer
blocks.note: read as an instruction on the letters: take AND out of the answer and a strong dark beer is left
the everyday phrasal verb for being conspicuous

annotation.surface: A brewing tip on how to make a beer that gets noticed.
annotation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: STAND with the AND out leaves ST, and STAND OUT minus AND leaves STOUT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain idiom: something conspicuous rises above the crowd, and the beer half is wordplay on the letters.

entries.clue: Fit is loose, but not very (4)

indicatorNotes.but not: the word without the letter that follows

annotation.surface: A garment's fit is baggy, though only slightly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like how clothes sit; it is a fit of shivering.
annotation.definitionFit: An ague is a fever with fits of shivering.

entries.clue: Part of cleaner space secured by, primarily, bargaining power (10)

indicatorNotes.secured by: held in place by what surrounds it
indicatorNotes.primarily: primarily means in the first place, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: the stick is force, as in carrot and stick

annotation.surface: A cleaning company whose office was won through tough negotiation.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bargaining power' reads as one phrase, but the commas cut 'primarily, bargaining' off as a single initial, and 'power' stands alone as the threat of force.
annotation.definitionFit: The broomstick is the handle, part of a broom, a cleaning tool.

entries.clue: Perhaps courtyard’s prisoners finally free, seemingly? (7)

indicatorNotes.finally: finally means at the end, so only the word's last letter is used

blocks.note: untrap looks as if it means to free; the ? admits it is a made-up word

annotation.surface: Inmates in a prison yard at last being released.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seemingly' concedes that UNTRAP is not a real word, only one that looks like 'free'.
annotation.definitionFit: A sheltered courtyard that catches sunshine is a suntrap.

entries.clue: Incur PAYE changes — fiscal (9)

annotation.surface: Tax changes that land you with more deductions from your pay.
annotation.walkthrough: PAYE is Pay As You Earn, British income tax taken from wages, which suits 'fiscal' perfectly.
annotation.definitionFit: Pecuniary means relating to money, much as fiscal does.

entries.clue: Feel less enamoured? Caught John backing away (4,3)

indicatorNotes.backing: going backwards, so read right to left

blocks.note: john is slang for a toilet, a loo

annotation.surface: Someone losing interest after catching John sidling away.
annotation.walkthrough: 'John' looks like a lover's name; it is a toilet.
annotation.definitionFit: To cool off towards someone is to feel less keen on them.

entries.clue: Improving working idea with no date (2,3,4)

blocks.note: a machine that is on is working
a theme is a central idea
n.d. = no date, as in bibliographies

annotation.surface: Honing a working idea that has no deadline yet.
annotation.walkthrough: N.D. is the standard note in a reference list for an undated source.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: a patient getting better after illness is said to be mending, like a repaired garment.

entries.clue: New student nurse cracks means to enhance atmosphere? (9)

indicatorNotes.cracks: the letters crack open the other word and sit inside

blocks.note: a fresher is a first-year student

annotation.surface: A first-year and a nurse finding ways to liven up a party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Atmosphere' sounds like a party's mood; the ? admits it means the air in a room.
annotation.definitionFit: An air freshener improves the atmosphere in a room.

entries.clue: Retailer wickedly smuggles port in Scotland (7)

indicatorNotes.smuggles: the words carry the answer hidden inside them

annotation.surface: A crooked shopkeeper running contraband into a Scottish harbour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smuggles' and 'port' make a perfect contraband scene, with the answer smuggled in plain sight.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the chief town of the Shetland Isles is a harbour, and Shetland belongs to Scotland.

entries.clue: Novel clever story had lately spread (4,11,5)

annotation.surface: A new and clever book that has recently caught on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like 'new' before 'clever story'; it is the definition. The book's content makes 'spread' a sly choice.
annotation.definitionFit: Lady Chatterley's Lover is D H Lawrence's novel, famous for its 1960 obscenity trial.

entries.clue: Network of parasites drinking blood group dry (7)

indicatorNotes.drinking: one word drinks the other in

annotation.surface: A web of bloodsuckers draining a certain blood group dry.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like the result of the drinking; it is TT, teetotal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: crossed strips of wood or metal form a grid, a network of open squares.

entries.clue: Unemotional City bore endlessly reflected about nothing (7)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: each word loses its end letter
indicatorNotes.reflected: seen in a mirror, so read backwards
indicatorNotes.about: the pieces go around the O

annotation.surface: A dull City banker with nothing to say, forever reflecting on it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The City' is London's financial district, so 'City bore' is a tedious banker. 'Endlessly' trims both words.
annotation.definitionFit: Robotic means mechanical and without emotion.

entries.clue: Turns out orders, second of which reduced by 99 per cent (6)

indicatorNotes.reduced by 99 per cent: as a Roman numeral, D is 500; 99 per cent off leaves 5, V

blocks.clueFragment: second of which reduced by 99 per cent
blocks.note: the second letter D (500) becomes V (5)

annotation.surface: A company slashing a batch of orders by almost all of it.
annotation.walkthrough: The arithmetic works only in Roman numerals: D is 500, 1 per cent of that is 5, and 5 is V.
annotation.definitionFit: To evict tenants is to turn them out.

entries.clue: Caught churchmen propped up outside back of boozer (6)

indicatorNotes.propped up: in a down clue, raised up, so read bottom to top
indicatorNotes.outside: the reversed word sits outside the other letter
indicatorNotes.back of: the back of a word is its tail end, so only the final letter is used

annotation.surface: Clergymen propping up the bar round the back of a pub, then getting caught.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Propped up' paints drinkers at the bar; here it reverses DEANS. A boozer is British slang for a pub.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a snare is a wire trap, so anything taken in one has been caught.

entries.clue: Tax I stop in New York City (7)

annotation.surface: A tourist complaining about sales tax on a stopover in New York.
annotation.walkthrough: 'New York City' reads as one place; 'City' alone is the definition and 'in New York' marks CAN as American slang.
annotation.definitionFit: Vatican City is the city-state that is home to the Pope.

entries.clue: Measure of resistance shown by broadcaster hosting king’s caricaturist (8)

indicatorNotes.hosting: one word plays host to the other inside it

blocks.note: the Beeb is a nickname for the BBC
the ohm is the unit of electrical resistance

annotation.surface: A cartoonist appearing on the BBC with a satirical study of the king.
annotation.walkthrough: The Beeb is British slang for the BBC. Max Beerbohm was an Edwardian caricaturist and writer.
annotation.definitionFit: Max Beerbohm was a celebrated English caricaturist.

entries.clue: Young Irishman to resist old (5)

blocks.note: to buck a trend is to resist it

annotation.surface: A young Irish lad set on defying his elders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old' looks like the elder being resisted; it is only O.
annotation.definitionFit: Bucko is Irish slang for a young fellow, a lad.

entries.clue: Fool and half disregard delegate (6)

blocks.note: the first half of IGNORE, to disregard

annotation.surface: A fool who half ignores the person sent in his place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Disregard' is never spelt out: its synonym IGNORE is halved.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: handing a job to someone else is both, the verb sense of delegate.

entries.clue: Case made by European travel company (4)

blocks.note: TUI is a large European holiday company

annotation.surface: A suitcase manufactured by a European holiday firm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like luggage in a travel setting; an etui is a small ornamental case for needles.
annotation.definitionFit: An etui is a small decorative case for needles or cosmetics.

entries.clue: What’s hot country delivered? (5)

indicatorNotes.delivered?: a speech is delivered, so take the sound of the word

annotation.surface: A question about which country is in fashion, as delivered by a speaker.
annotation.walkthrough: Chile is cold at its southern end, so a hot chili sounding like it is the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the pepper is the classic hot thing, and 'What's hot' fits a question-shaped clue.

entries.clue: Decrepit worker, say, eats dainty with guts turning (7)

indicatorNotes.eats: one word eats the other, taking it inside
indicatorNotes.guts turning: the middle letters are turned round

blocks.note: a worker ant, the example the 'say' flags
nice = dainty, delicate; its guts IC turn to CI, giving NCIE

annotation.surface: An old worker tucking into a delicate treat that turns his stomach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Guts turning' sounds like nausea; it means only the middle letters of NICE are reversed.
annotation.definitionFit: Ancient means very old, decrepit.

entries.clue: Outside front of theatre with sleuth, pound knocker (9)

indicatorNotes.front of: the front of a word is its opening, so only the first letter is used

blocks.note: a PI is a private investigator
nicker is British slang for a pound sterling

annotation.surface: A detective loitering outside a theatre, hammering on the door.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pound knocker' reads as someone hammering on a door; 'knocker' is a critic and 'pound' is money.
annotation.definitionFit: A nitpicker is a petty critic, a knocker of small faults.

entries.clue: Hint of error in small (very small) point about duke’s killer (7,4)

indicatorNotes.Hint of: a hint of a word is its first letter
indicatorNotes.in: the letter goes inside the other words
indicatorNotes.about: the word turns about, reading backwards

blocks.note: weeny = tiny; the E goes in before its Y
